title: The European Union's external imbalances: past, future and policy
summary_en: The EU's current account moved from balanced in the early 2000s to a persistent ~3% of GDP surplus today — rivalling China's. Darvas and co-authors trace the shift to weak domestic investment in southern and eastern Europe, not to runaway exports, and argue demographic ageing will sustain the surplus into the future. They recommend business-environment reform, deeper capital-market integration, and fiscal-rule changes that allow more public investment.
policy_relevance: Directly relevant for Hungarian fiscal and investment-promotion strategy (NGM, ITM, MFB): the diagnosis blames thin domestic investment, not export performance, for the surplus — and Hungary fits the pattern. Suggests Hungarian policy should prioritise instruments that lift private investment (business-environment reform, scale-up financing, cap-market deepening) over export-promotion measures. Also supports Hungary's position in EU fiscal-rule debates that allow more space for public investment.
